claim: Planarian flatworms have an extensive stem cell population responsible for regenerating any organ after amputation.
source: Planarian flatworms have an extensive stem cell population responsible for regenerating any organ after amputation.
evidence: This is a foundational statement about planarian regenerative capacity, supported by established knowledge in the field and citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: Planarian stem cells adopt distinct behaviors depending on what tissue is missing to target progenitor and tissue production towards missing tissues.
source: We find that planarian stem cells adopt distinct behaviors depending on what tissue is missing to target progenitor and tissue production towards missing tissues.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript comparing stem cell responses to different injuries.

claim: Loss of non-pharyngeal tissues only increases non-pharyngeal progenitors.
source: Loss of non-pharyngeal tissues only increases non-pharyngeal progenitors, while pharynx removal selectively triggers division and expansion of pharynx progenitors.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing differential progenitor responses to different types of tissue removal.

claim: Pharynx removal selectively triggers division and expansion of pharynx progenitors.
source: Loss of non-pharyngeal tissues only increases non-pharyngeal progenitors, while pharynx removal selectively triggers division and expansion of pharynx progenitors.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing increased FoxA+ progenitors after pharynx amputation.

claim: There is a narrow window of time (1-2 days after amputation) during which stem cell division produces pharynx progenitors necessary for regeneration.
source: By pharmacologically inhibiting either mitosis or activation of the MAP kinase ERK, we identify a narrow window of time during which stem cell division and ERK signaling produces pharynx progenitors necessary for regeneration.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data using nocodazole and MEK inhibitors at different time points.

claim: ERK signaling within a critical window (1-2 days after amputation) produces pharynx progenitors necessary for regeneration.
source: By pharmacologically inhibiting either mitosis or activation of the MAP kinase ERK, we identify a narrow window of time during which stem cell division and ERK signaling produces pharynx progenitors necessary for regeneration.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data using PD0325901 and UO126 at different time points after amputation.

claim: Planarian stem cells can tailor their output to match the regenerative needs of the animal.
source: These results indicate that planarian stem cells can tailor their output to match the regenerative needs of the animal.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing selective progenitor responses to different injuries.

claim: In adult mammals, injuries to the intestine, skin, or lung induce stem cells to increase proliferation rates and alter their differentiation potential.
source: For example, in adult mammals, injuries to the intestine, skin, or lung induce stem cells to increase proliferation rates and alter their differentiation potential (Buczacki et al., 2013; Stabler and Morrisey, 2017; Tetteh et al., 2015; Tumbar et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The planarian stem cell population is defined by ubiquitous expression of the argonaute transcript piwi-1.
source: Defined by ubiquitous expression of the argonaute transcript piwi-1 (Reddien et al., 2005), the planarian stem cell population consists of pluripotent stem cells capable of reconstituting the entire animal (Wagner et al., 2011) and likely organ-specific progenitors (Figure 1A; Scimone et al., 2014a; van Wolfswinkel et al., 2014; Zeng et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Reddien et al., 2005 and is established knowledge in the field.

claim: The planarian stem cell population consists of pluripotent stem cells capable of reconstituting the entire animal.
source: Defined by ubiquitous expression of the argonaute transcript piwi-1 (Reddien et al., 2005), the planarian stem cell population consists of pluripotent stem cells capable of reconstituting the entire animal (Wagner et al., 2011) and likely organ-specific progenitors (Figure 1A; Scimone et al., 2014a; van Wolfswinkel et al., 2014; Zeng et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wagner et al., 2011.

claim: The planarian stem cell population likely includes organ-specific progenitors.
source: Defined by ubiquitous expression of the argonaute transcript piwi-1 (Reddien et al., 2005), the planarian stem cell population consists of pluripotent stem cells capable of reconstituting the entire animal (Wagner et al., 2011) and likely organ-specific progenitors (Figure 1A; Scimone et al., 2014a; van Wolfswinkel et al., 2014; Zeng et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations and Figure 1A showing the stem cell lineage.

claim: The pharynx can be completely and selectively removed without perturbing other tissues by brief exposure to sodium azide.
source: Importantly, it can be completely and selectively removed without perturbing other tissues by brief exposure to sodium azide (Figure 1B; Adler et al., 2014; Shiroor et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations and Figure 1B showing live images before and after pharynx amputation.

claim: Pharynx amputation triggers an increase in FoxA+ stem cells.
source: Pharynx amputation triggers an increase in FoxA+ stem cells, demonstrating that injury expands the pool of pharynx progenitors.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and previous citations (Adler et al., 2014; Scimone et al., 2014a).

claim: Within hours of any injury, a general increase in stem cell division occurs, along with vast transcriptional changes.
source: Within hours of any injury, a general increase in stem cell division occurs, along with vast transcriptional changes (Baguñà, 1976; Gaviño et al., 2013; Sandmann et al., 2011; Wenemoser et al., 2012; Wenemoser and Reddien, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Injury-induced changes in stem cells are only sustained beyond the first day if tissue is removed, in what is referred to as the 'missing tissue response'.
source: These changes are only sustained beyond the first day if tissue is removed, in what is referred to as the 'missing tissue response' (Baguñà, 1976; Gaviño et al., 2013; Wenemoser and Reddien, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: ERK contributes to many wound-induced transcriptional changes, in addition to regulating stem cell proliferation, differentiation, and survival.
source: Activated by injury, the extracellular signal-regulated kinase (ERK) contributes to many of these wound-induced transcriptional changes, in addition to regulating stem cell proliferation, differentiation, and survival (Owlarn et al., 2017; Shiroor et al., 2020; Tasaki et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: FoxA is expressed in the pharynx and a subset of stem cells under homeostatic conditions.
source: Under homeostatic conditions, FoxA is expressed in the pharynx and a subset of stem cells.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge and previous work cited in the manuscript.

claim: F-ara-EdU administration immediately after amputation (D0) resulted in increased F-ara-EdU+ cells in the pharynx following either pharynx or head removal, compared to intact controls.
source: When F-ara-EdU was applied immediately after amputation (D0), we observed increased F-ara-EdU+ cells in the pharynx following either pharynx or head removal, as compared to intact controls (Figure 1E,F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E,F.

claim: F-ara-EdU administration 1 day after amputation (D1) resulted in a specific increase in F-ara-EdU+ pharynx cells only after removal of the pharynx, but not the head.
source: However, F-ara-EdU administration 1 day after amputation (D1) resulted in a specific increase in F-ara-EdU+ pharynx cells only after removal of the pharynx, but not the head (Figure 1E,F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E,F.

claim: Incisions anterior to the pharynx that damaged the body without removing any tissue did not increase F-ara-EdU+ cells in the pharynx compared to controls.
source: However, the number of F-ara-EdU+ cells in the pharynx were comparable to controls, suggesting that tissue removal strongly stimulates production of new tissue, while injury alone does not.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing incisions to amputations.

claim: Tissue removal strongly stimulates production of new tissue, while injury alone does not.
source: However, the number of F-ara-EdU+ cells in the pharynx were comparable to controls, suggesting that tissue removal strongly stimulates production of new tissue, while injury alone does not.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from experimental data comparing incisions to amputations.

claim: In the newly regenerated brain, head amputation increased F-ara-EdU+ ChAT+ neurons after both F-ara-EdU pulse conditions (D0 and D1), compared to intact controls.
source: In the newly regenerated brain, head amputation increased F-ara-EdU+ ChAT+ neurons after both F-ara-EdU pulse conditions, as compared to intact controls.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: The number of F-ara-EdU+ ChAT+ brain neurons were comparable to controls after either pharynx amputation or incisions, regardless of when the F-ara-EdU pulse was administered.
source: However, the number of F-ara-EdU+ ChAT+ brain neurons were comparable to controls after either pharynx amputation or incisions, regardless of when the F-ara-EdU pulse was administered (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: Cells generated immediately after tissue removal can be broadly deployed to all surrounding tissues, while those generated 1 day later are targeted toward only those that are missing.
source: These results suggest that while cells generated immediately after tissue removal can be broadly deployed to all surrounding tissues, those generated 1 day later are targeted toward only those that are missing.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the F-ara-EdU labeling experiments at different time points.

claim: Pharynx removal caused a significant increase in pharynx progenitors (FoxA+ piwi-1+ cells) 3 days after amputation compared to intact controls.
source: As previously reported, we found that pharynx removal caused a significant increase in pharynx progenitors as compared to intact controls (Adler et al., 2014; Scimone et al., 2014a).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and previous citations.

claim: Head amputation did not influence the number of pharynx progenitors, which were similar to intact animals.
source: By contrast, head amputation did not influence the number of pharynx progenitors, which were similar to intact animals (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A,B.

claim: Pharynx progenitors significantly increased 3 days after pharynx amputation.
source: Because injury broadly influences stem cell behavior, we also analyzed the proportion of these pharynx progenitors relative to all other piwi-1+ stem cells at the same times after pharynx and head amputation and found a similar trend (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B). These data indicate that pharynx progenitors are selectively produced 3 days after pharynx loss, but not after loss of other tissue types.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Incisions that damaged the pharynx without removing any tissue failed to stimulate an increase in piwi-1+FoxA+ stem cells.
source: Incisions that damaged the pharynx without removing any tissue failed to stimulate an increase in piwi-1+FoxA + stem cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Partial removal of the pharynx (~50–80%) caused a significant increase in pharynx progenitors compared to intact controls.
source: However, partial removal of the pharynx (~50–80%) caused a significant increase in pharynx progenitors compared to intact controls.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Flank resections, which removed tissue from regions adjacent to the pharynx but did not damage the pharynx itself, resulted in comparable numbers of pharynx progenitors as in intact controls.
source: We also performed flank resections, which removed tissue from regions adjacent to the pharynx but did not damage the pharynx itself. Despite being previously shown to increase new cells into the uninjured pharynx with BrdU labeling (LoCascio et al., 2017), we observed comparable numbers of pharynx progenitors as in intact controls (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D and contrasts with previous findings.

claim: Stimulation of pharynx progenitor production is local and requires recognition of lost pharynx tissue, but not necessarily loss of the entire organ.
source: These data suggest that stimulation of pharynx progenitor production is local and requires recognition of lost pharynx tissue, but not necessarily loss of the entire organ.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from experimental data showing regional and injury-specific responses.

claim: Following pharynx amputation, eye progenitors (ovo+ piwi-1+) did not increase.
source: Conversely, following pharynx amputation, this increase did not occur (Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplement 2A), indicating that pharynx loss does not stimulate the production of eye progenitors.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Muscle (myoD+), excretory system (six-1/2+), and nervous system (pax6a+) progenitors increased within 3 days after head removal, but not pharynx removal.
source: With the exception of intestinal progenitors, all others showed a similar behavior, increasing within 3 days after head removal, but not pharynx removal (Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplement 2B–E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 2B–E.

claim: Intestinal progenitors (gata-4/5/6+) did not show increased numbers after either pharynx or head removal.
source: With the exception of intestinal progenitors, all others showed a similar behavior, increasing within 3 days after head removal, but not pharynx removal (Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplement 2B–E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 2B–E.

claim: No changes in organ-specific progenitors were observed in tail regions after pharynx or head amputation, indicating that it is a local response.
source: No changes in any of these organ-specific progenitors were observed in tail regions after pharynx or head amputation, indicating that it is a local response (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Planarian stem cells sense the loss of missing tissues to initiate their regeneration through the selective expansion of organ-specific progenitors.
source: Together, these data indicate that planarian stem cells sense the loss of missing tissues to initiate their regeneration through the selective expansion of organ-specific progenitors.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing selective progenitor responses.

claim: FoxA is required for pharynx regeneration.
source: Unlike FoxA(RNAi), knockdown of other organ-specific progenitor markers did not impact the recovery of feeding ability (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A), despite efficient knockdown and manifestation of known phenotypes (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B, data not shown).
evidence: This is supported by RNAi experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Knockdown of ovo, myoD, six-1/2, pax6a, gata-4/5/6, or coe did not impact the recovery of feeding ability after pharynx amputation.
source: Unlike FoxA(RNAi), knockdown of other organ-specific progenitor markers did not impact the recovery of feeding ability (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A), despite efficient knockdown and manifestation of known phenotypes (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B, data not shown).
evidence: This is supported by RNAi experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Stem cell division increased near wounds beginning 1 day after either pharynx or head removal.
source: Using this mitotic marker, we verified that stem cell division increased near wounds beginning 1 day after either pharynx or head removal (Figure 3A; Adler et al., 2014; Baguñà, 1976).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A and previous citations.

claim: One day after pharynx removal, higher numbers of H3P+ pharynx progenitors (FoxA+ H3P+) were observed in regions adjacent to wounds compared to intact animals.
source: One day after pharynx removal, we observed higher numbers of H3P+ pharynx progenitors in regions adjacent to wounds as compared to intact animals (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Division of pharynx progenitors increased within 6 hr of pharynx amputation, peaked within 2 days, and returned to homeostatic levels by 5 days after amputation.
source: Division of pharynx progenitors increased within 6 hr of pharynx amputation, peaked within 2 days, and returned to homeostatic levels by 5 days after amputation (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Despite an overall increase in H3P+ stem cells 1 day after head amputation, numbers of H3P+ pharynx progenitors did not correspondingly increase.
source: Despite an overall increase in H3P+ stem cells 1 day after head amputation (Figure 3A; Baguñà, 1976), numbers of H3P+ pharynx progenitors did not correspondingly increase (Figure 3B,D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B,D and previous citation.

claim: Pharynx progenitors are selectively stimulated to divide in response to pharynx loss.
source: Together, these data show that pharynx progenitors are selectively stimulated to divide in response to pharynx loss.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experimental data comparing pharynx and head amputations.

claim: Instances of both symmetric and asymmetric distribution of FoxA in cells undergoing anaphase were observed.
source: Interestingly, we were able to detect what appeared to be instances of both symmetric and asymmetric distribution of FoxA in cells undergoing anaphase (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Excretory system (six1/2+), nervous system (pax6a+), and muscle (myoD+) progenitor division increased 2 days after head amputation.
source: Although the kinetics of each differed slightly, excretory system (six1/2+), nervous system (pax6a+), and muscle (myoD+) progenitor division increased 2 days after head amputation, while intestinal (gata-4/5/6+) progenitors did not.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–D.

claim: Intestinal (gata-4/5/6+) progenitor division did not increase after head amputation.
source: Although the kinetics of each differed slightly, excretory system (six1/2+), nervous system (pax6a+), and muscle (myoD+) progenitor division increased 2 days after head amputation, while intestinal (gata-4/5/6+) progenitors did not.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 2D.

claim: Division of nervous system and muscle progenitors increased only after head but not pharynx amputation.
source: Additionally, division of nervous system and muscle progenitors increased only after head but not pharynx amputation (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–D.

claim: Loss of non-pharyngeal tissues triggers division of stem cells expressing non-pharyngeal progenitor markers while in most cases, pharynx loss does not.
source: Despite minor differences of each progenitor, the overall trend supports the notion that loss of non-pharyngeal tissues triggers division of stem cells expressing non-pharyngeal progenitor markers while in most cases, pharynx loss does not.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experimental data on multiple progenitor types.

claim: Increased division of organ-specific progenitors was not observed in tail regions, distant from wounds.
source: This mitotic response appears again to be local, as we did not observe increased division of any of these organ-specific progenitors in tail regions, distant from wounds (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A–D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3A–D.

claim: Dividing eye progenitors (ovo+H3P+) were not detected after head amputation unless mitotic exit was stalled with nocodazole.
source: Even after head amputation, we were unable to detect any dividing eye progenitors (ovo+H3P+) (Figure 3—figure supplement 4A), unless we stalled mitotic exit with the microtubule destabilizing drug nocodazole.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4A,B.

claim: Eye progenitors divide, but their division dynamics do not seem to be affected by injury.
source: Therefore, while eye progenitors do divide, their division dynamics do not seem to be affected by injury, similar to intestinal progenitors (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from experimental data on eye progenitor division.

claim: There may be other eye and intestinal progenitors upstream of those expressing ovo or gata-4/5/6, or expansion of these progenitors may occur via transcriptional upregulation.
source: This finding suggests that there may be other eye and intestinal progenitors upstream of those expressing ovo or gata-4/5/6, or that expansion of these progenitors may occur via transcriptional upregulation.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation that these progenitors do not show increased division after injury.

claim: Animals treated with nocodazole for 24 hr beginning 1 day after pharynx amputation had drastic delays in recovery of feeding, with only 50% of worms regaining the ability to eat within 20 days, and 100% within 32 days of amputation.
source: Animals treated with nocodazole for 24 hr had drastic delays in recovery of feeding, compared to DMSO-treated controls, with only 50% of worms regaining the ability to eat within 20 days, and 100% within 32 days of amputation (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Animals treated with nocodazole 1–2 days after pharynx amputation completely lacked a pharynx with its characteristic layered structure 7 days after amputation and sustained severe defects even up to 14 days.
source: As expected, while residual laminin expression was retained within the body, animals treated with nocodazole 1–2 days after pharynx amputation completely lacked a pharynx with its characteristic layered structure 7 days after amputation and sustained severe defects even up to 14 days (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Treatment with nocodazole for a full 48 hr, beginning immediately after amputation, did not exacerbate the delay in feeding ability or defects in pharynx anatomy compared to 24 hr treatment starting 1 day after amputation.
source: Treatment with nocodazole for a full 48 hr, beginning immediately after amputation (Figure 4B), did not exacerbate the delay in feeding ability or defects in pharynx anatomy (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C,D.

claim: Stem cell division outside the 1–2 day window has a minor contribution to pharynx regeneration.
source: These findings suggest that stem cell division outside the 1–2 day window has a minor contribution to pharynx regeneration.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from nocodazole treatment experiments at different time windows.

claim: Animals treated with nocodazole from 0 to 1 days after amputation had only minor defects in pharynx anatomy, while those treated 2–3 days after amputation were normal.
source: Further, animals treated from 0 to 1 days after amputation had only minor defects in pharynx anatomy, while those treated 2–3 days after amputation were normal (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Stem cell division within a critical window of 1–2 days after amputation fuels the majority of pharynx regeneration.
source: Therefore, we conclude that stem cell division within a critical window of 1–2 days after amputation fuels the majority of pharynx regeneration.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from nocodazole treatment experiments at different time windows.

claim: Nocodazole treatment 1–2 days after pharynx amputation caused a dramatic decrease in pharynx progenitors (FoxA+ piwi-1+ cells) 3 days after pharynx removal compared to controls.
source: Second, we performed double FISH for FoxA and piwi-1 3 days after pharynx removal and found that nocodazole treatment caused a dramatic decrease in pharynx progenitors compared to controls (Figure 4E,F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E,F.

claim: Intact animals treated with nocodazole showed no difference in the abundance of pharynx progenitors compared to controls.
source: Importantly, intact animals treated similarly with nocodazole showed no difference in the abundance of pharynx progenitors compared to controls (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C,D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2C,D.

claim: Perturbing stem cell division during the 1-2 day window specifically impacts the production of pharynx progenitors during regeneration.
source: Therefore, perturbing stem cell division during this brief window specifically impacts the production of pharynx progenitors during regeneration.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from nocodazole treatment experiments.

claim: Stem cell division in a critical window of 1–2 days after amputation produces pharynx progenitors that are likely essential for pharynx regeneration.
source: Together, our data show that stem cell division in a critical window of 1–2 days after amputation produces pharynx progenitors that are likely essential for pharynx regeneration.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from nocodazole treatment experiments showing effects on both progenitors and regeneration.

claim: pERK increased 15 min after pharynx amputation and returned to baseline levels within 6 hr.
source: pERK increased 15 min after pharynx amputation and returned to baseline levels within 6 hr (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Pharynx amputation activates ERK by phosphorylation soon after injury, similar to other injuries.
source: Therefore, similar to other injuries (Owlarn et al., 2017), pharynx amputation also activates ERK by phosphorylation soon after injury.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data and citation to Owlarn et al., 2017.

claim: Animals treated with PD0325901 (PD) from 0 to 5 days after pharynx amputation had substantial delays in feeding, with 50% of worms feeding by day 13 and all worms feeding by day 29.
source: While DMSO-treated control animals regained the ability to feed within 7 days, animals treated with PD from 0 to 5 days after amputation had substantial delays in feeding, with 50% of worms feeding by day 13 and all worms feeding by day 29 (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Animals exposed to PD0325901 1 day after pharynx amputation (1–6 days) had delayed feeding ability, similar to those treated immediately after amputation (0–5 days).
source: Animals exposed 1 day after pharynx amputation (1–6 days) had delayed feeding ability, similar to those treated immediately after amputation (0–5 days), suggesting that ERK activity within the first day of amputation is dispensable for pharynx regeneration.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Animals exposed to PD0325901 2 days after amputation (2–7 days) regained the ability to feed at rates similar to controls.
source: Animals exposed 2 days after amputation (2–7 days) regained the ability to feed at rates similar to controls (Figure 5C), indicating that ERK is essential for regeneration within the first 2 days after pharynx amputation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: ERK is essential for pharynx regeneration within the first 2 days after pharynx amputation.
source: Animals exposed 2 days after amputation (2–7 days) regained the ability to feed at rates similar to controls (Figure 5C), indicating that ERK is essential for regeneration within the first 2 days after pharynx amputation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from PD0325901 treatment experiments at different time windows.

claim: ERK likely acts primarily between 1 and 2 days after pharynx amputation.
source: Therefore, ERK likely acts primarily between 1 and 2 days after pharynx amputation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from PD0325901 treatment experiments showing dispensability of ERK in the first day.

claim: Pharynx regeneration may be facilitated by homeostatic levels of ERK signaling instead of its injury-induced high level activation.
source: This timing occurs after the increase in pERK following injury has already subsided (Figure 5A), suggesting that pharynx regeneration may be facilitated by homeostatic levels of ERK signaling instead of its injury-induced high level activation.
evidence: This is speculation based on the timing of ERK requirement relative to pERK levels.

claim: Animals exposed to PD for 5 days, beginning 0 or 1 day after amputation, lacked a pharynx 7 days after pharynx amputation, while pharynges in animals exposed beginning 2 days after amputation were comparable to controls.
source: Animals exposed to PD for 5 days, beginning 0 or 1 day after amputation, lacked a pharynx, while pharynges in animals exposed beginning 2 days after amputation were comparable to controls (Figure 5D), mirroring the results of our feeding assay (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: PD-exposed animals eventually regenerated a pharynx within about 2 weeks.
source: PD-exposed animals eventually regenerated a pharynx within about 2 weeks (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), suggesting that ERK inhibition does not permanently block pharynx regeneration.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: ERK inhibition does not permanently block pharynx regeneration.
source: PD-exposed animals eventually regenerated a pharynx within about 2 weeks (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), suggesting that ERK inhibition does not permanently block pharynx regeneration.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that PD-treated animals eventually regenerate.

claim: UO126, another MEK inhibitor, produced the same outcomes as PD0325901 in pharynx regeneration experiments.
source: Therefore, we confirmed the effects of ERK inhibition by repeating pharynx regeneration experiments with UO126 (UO), another potent, but structurally independent, MEK inhibitor and observed the same outcomes (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B–D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B–D.

claim: Exposure to PD or UO eliminated pERK after pharynx amputation.
source: Furthermore, exposure to PD or UO eliminated pERK after pharynx amputation on a western blot (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E) and also permanently blocked regeneration after extensive anterior tissue removal, for up to 70 days (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Exposure to PD or UO permanently blocked regeneration after extensive anterior tissue removal, for up to 70 days.
source: Furthermore, exposure to PD or UO eliminated pERK after pharynx amputation on a western blot (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E) and also permanently blocked regeneration after extensive anterior tissue removal, for up to 70 days (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1F.

claim: fst expression increases within 6 hr of head amputation.
source: To test this, we analyzed fst expression, which increases within 6 hr of head amputation (Gaviño et al., 2013), but not until 24 hr after pharynx amputation (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A), suggesting that injury-induced ERK activation (Figure 5A) may not always coincide with fst upregulation.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gaviño et al., 2013 and experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A.

claim: fst expression increases 24 hr after pharynx amputation.
source: To test this, we analyzed fst expression, which increases within 6 hr of head amputation (Gaviño et al., 2013), but not until 24 hr after pharynx amputation (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A), suggesting that injury-induced ERK activation (Figure 5A) may not always coincide with fst upregulation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Injury-induced ERK activation may not always coincide with fst upregulation.
source: To test this, we analyzed fst expression, which increases within 6 hr of head amputation (Gaviño et al., 2013), but not until 24 hr after pharynx amputation (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A), suggesting that injury-induced ERK activation (Figure 5A) may not always coincide with fst upregulation.
evidence: This is speculation based on the timing differences between pERK and fst expression.

claim: fst is not required to accelerate pharynx regeneration.
source: Despite upregulation of fst expression after pharynx amputation, fst(RNAi) animals regained the ability to feed at a normal rate (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B and C), indicating that fst is not required to accelerate pharynx regeneration.
evidence: This is supported by RNAi experiments shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B and C.

claim: Regulation of pharynx regeneration via ERK is independent of fst.
source: Therefore, although pharynx loss eventually induces fst expression, regulation of pharynx regeneration via ERK is independent of fst.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from fst RNAi experiments showing no effect on pharynx regeneration.

claim: PD exposure for 3 days following pharynx amputation significantly inhibited the increase in FoxA+ piwi-1+ cells typically observed after pharynx amputation.
source: PD exposure significantly inhibited the increase in FoxA+ piwi-1+ cells typically observed after pharynx amputation (Figure 5E,F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E,F.

claim: Intact animals treated with PD for 3 days showed no difference in the abundance of pharynx progenitors as compared to controls.
source: Importantly, intact animals treated with PD for 3 days showed no difference in the abundance of pharynx progenitors as compared to controls (Figure 5—figure supplement 3A), indicating that ERK activity for this duration is not necessary for maintaining pharynx progenitors during homeostasis.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3A.

claim: ERK activity for 3 days is not necessary for maintaining pharynx progenitors during homeostasis.
source: Importantly, intact animals treated with PD for 3 days showed no difference in the abundance of pharynx progenitors as compared to controls (Figure 5—figure supplement 3A), indicating that ERK activity for this duration is not necessary for maintaining pharynx progenitors during homeostasis.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from PD treatment experiments in intact animals.

claim: The decrease in pharynx progenitors following pharynx amputation and PD treatment is likely due to their reduced production, rather than altered survival.
source: Therefore, the decrease in pharynx progenitors following pharynx amputation and PD treatment is likely due to their reduced production, rather than altered survival.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that PD does not affect progenitors in intact animals.

claim: PD treatment starting 1 day after pharynx amputation significantly inhibited pharynx progenitor increase, similar to those treated for three full days.
source: While PD treatment starting 0 or 2 days after pharynx amputation had no effect on pharynx progenitors, treatment starting 1 day after amputation significantly inhibited pharynx progenitor increase, similar to those treated for three full days (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: ERK activity 1–2 days after pharynx amputation promotes the production of pharynx progenitors during regeneration.
source: Similar experiments with UO yielded the same outcomes (Figure 5—figure supplement 3A,B), demonstrating that ERK activity 1–2 days after pharynx amputation promotes the production of pharynx progenitors during regeneration.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from PD and UO treatment experiments at different time windows.

claim: Animals exposed to PD for 0–3 days and 1–2 days after amputation had delays in feeding, although less severe than those treated for five full days.
source: These animals had delays in feeding, although less severe than those treated for five full days (Figure 5—figure supplement 3C), presumably because animals start recovering after drug washout.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3C.

claim: Animals treated with PD for 0–1 day after pharynx amputation recovered feeding ability at normal rates.
source: Meanwhile, those treated for 0–1 day after pharynx amputation recovered feeding ability at normal rates (Figure 5—figure supplement 3C), illustrating that PD exposure that does not affect the production of pharynx progenitors does not delay regeneration.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3C.

claim: ERK activity 1–2 days after amputation promotes pharynx regeneration by contributing to the increase in pharynx progenitors 3 days after amputation.
source: Together, these results indicate that ERK activity 1–2 days after amputation promotes pharynx regeneration by contributing to the increase in pharynx progenitors 3 days after amputation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from PD treatment experiments showing effects on both progenitors and regeneration.

claim: Neither PD nor UO exposure substantially impacted the number of dividing pharynx progenitors (FoxA+ H3P+) compared to controls.
source: Neither PD or UO exposure substantially impacted the number of dividing pharynx progenitors as compared to controls (Figure 5G,H, Figure 5—figure supplement 3D), despite an overall decrease in H3P+ stem cells in the same animals (Figure 5—figure supplement 3E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5G,H and Figure 5—figure supplement 3D.

claim: ERK signaling is not required for the selective increase in pharynx progenitor division induced by pharynx loss.
source: These data indicate that ERK signaling is not required for the selective increase in pharynx progenitor division induced by pharynx loss.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from PD/UO treatment experiments showing no effect on pharynx progenitor division.

claim: ERK is unlikely to regulate initiation of pharynx progenitor division.
source: Because the timing of ERK's requirement for increasing pharynx progenitors overlaps with when stem cell division is required (Figure 4C–F) 1–2 days after pharynx removal, ERK signaling is unlikely to regulate initiation of pharynx progenitor division.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the timing of ERK and division requirements.

claim: ERK likely promotes pharynx progenitor production and regeneration by regulating FoxA expression and stem cell differentiation.
source: Instead, ERK likely promotes pharynx progenitor production and regeneration by regulating FoxA expression and stem cell differentiation.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation that ERK affects progenitor numbers but not division.

claim: Eye regeneration following selective removal does not depend on stem cell division or ERK signaling.
source: Exposure to either nocodazole for 2 days, or MEK inhibitors for 5 days, did not impact eye regeneration (Figure 6B,C), despite a complete block of pharynx regeneration under these conditions (Figure 4D, Figure 5D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B,C.

claim: Eye regeneration is unaffected by drug treatments that block pharynx regeneration.
source: Our results show that, unlike pharynx regeneration, eye regeneration does not require stem cell division or ERK activity after selective removal.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from drug treatment experiments on eye regeneration.

claim: Pre-existing eye progenitors, or the continued production of homeostatic levels of eye progenitors, is sufficient for eye regeneration following selective removal.
source: Therefore, it is possible that pre-existing eye progenitors, or more likely, the continued production of homeostatic levels of eye progenitors (LoCascio et al., 2017) is sufficient for eye regeneration following selective removal.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation that eye regeneration does not require injury-induced responses.

claim: Eye regeneration requires stem cell division and ERK signaling in the context of more severe injuries (head amputation).
source: By contrast, animals treated with either nocodazole for 2 days or ERK inhibitors for 5 days failed to regenerate eyes, despite the presence of ovo+ eye progenitors (Figure 6D,E). We conclude that unlike pharynx regeneration, eye regeneration only requires stem cell division and ERK signaling in the context of more severe injuries.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D,E.

claim: Different injuries may require distinct regenerative mechanisms.
source: Unlike the pharynx, eye regeneration following selective removal is not dependent on stem cell division or ERK signaling, suggesting that different injuries may require distinct regenerative mechanisms.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing pharynx and eye regeneration requirements.

claim: Stem cells can sense the identity of missing tissues.
source: By performing an in-depth analysis of specific populations of stem cells in response to different injuries, we show that stem cells can sense the identity of missing tissues.
evidence: This is a major conclusion of the study supported by experimental data on selective progenitor responses.

claim: Stem cells respond to organ loss by selectively increasing expression of organ-specific transcription factors required for subsequent regeneration.
source: Planarian stem cells respond to organ loss by selectively increasing expression of organ-specific transcription factors required for subsequent regeneration.
evidence: This is a major conclusion of the study supported by experimental data on progenitor marker expression.

claim: Amputation of non-pharyngeal tissues only amplifies non-pharyngeal progenitors.
source: Amputation of non-pharyngeal tissues only amplifies non-pharyngeal progenitors, while removal of pharynx tissue selectively increases pharynx progenitors.
evidence: This is a major conclusion of the study supported by experimental data on different progenitor types.

claim: The increase in pharynx progenitors, and subsequent pharynx regeneration, depends on stem cell division and the MAP kinase ERK, during defined times after tissue loss.
source: This increase in pharynx progenitors, and subsequent pharynx regeneration, depends on stem cell division and the MAP kinase ERK, during defined times after tissue loss.
evidence: This is a major conclusion of the study supported by drug treatment experiments.

claim: In addition to non-targeted and passive modes of regeneration, stem cell behavior can be altered by the loss of specific tissues, selectively channeling their output towards replacement of missing organs.
source: We propose that, in addition to non-targeted and passive modes of regeneration, stem cell behavior can be altered by the loss of specific tissues, selectively channeling their output towards replacement of missing organs.
evidence: This is a major conclusion and proposal of the study based on all experimental findings.

claim: Depending on the type of injury, cells generated soon after amputation are channeled into all nearby tissues, even undamaged ones.
source: Depending on the type of injury, cells generated soon after amputation are channeled into all nearby tissues, even undamaged ones.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from F-ara-EdU labeling experiments at D0.

claim: Cells generated 1 day after amputation are selectively targeted for missing tissues.
source: However, those generated 1 day after amputation are selectively targeted for missing tissues.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from F-ara-EdU labeling experiments at D1.

claim: The timing of the targeted mechanism overlaps with an essential peak in pharynx progenitor division.
source: Importantly, the timing of this targeted mechanism overlaps with an essential peak in pharynx progenitor division, revealing that this mechanism generates organ progenitors necessary for the replacement of missing tissues.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing F-ara-EdU labeling and H3P staining timelines.

claim: The cells that regenerate the pharynx are primarily generated through a targeted mechanism, mediated by stem cell division and ERK signaling between 1 and 2 days after amputation.
source: The cells that regenerate the pharynx are primarily generated through this targeted mechanism, mediated by stem cell division and ERK signaling between 1and 2 days after amputation (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a major conclusion of the study supported by multiple lines of experimental evidence.

claim: Smaller lesions, such as eye resections, do not stimulate a proliferative wound response.
source: Smaller lesions, such as eye resections, do not stimulate a proliferative wound response (LoCascio et al., 2017), nor do they depend on stem cell division and ERK signaling for subsequent regeneration.
evidence: This is supported by citation and experimental data on eye regeneration.

claim: If eye removal is not detected as an injury, and is insufficient to trigger a 'missing tissue signal', this could explain why eye regeneration happens passively via homeostatic cellular turnover.
source: If eye removal is not detected as an injury, and is insufficient to trigger a 'missing tissue signal', this could explain why eye regeneration, following resection, happens passively via homeostatic cellular turnover in the regenerating eye (LoCascio et al., 2017).
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation that eye resection does not trigger typical injury responses.

claim: Non-targeted regeneration may require injury to specific types of tissues, such as body wall muscle or epithelia, in addition to tissue loss.
source: Further, while surgical removal of the pharynx does increase production of neural tissue (LoCascio et al., 2017), selective chemical pharynx removal does not, suggesting that non-targeted regeneration may require injury to specific types of tissues, such as body wall muscle or epithelia, in addition to tissue loss.
evidence: This is speculation based on comparing surgical and chemical pharynx removal.

claim: Multiple avenues lead to regeneration: passive homeostatic turnover in the absence of typical injury responses, and both targeted and non-targeted mechanisms that increase cellular production when tissue is lost.
source: Therefore, multiple avenues lead to regeneration: passive homeostatic turnover in the absence of typical injury responses, and both targeted and non-targeted mechanisms that increase cellular production when tissue is lost.
evidence: This is a major conclusion of the study integrating all findings on different regeneration modes.

claim: Depending on the size and severity of the wound, initial injury signals may vary, triggering a differential requirement for stem cell division and regulatory signaling pathways.
source: In particular, depending on the size and severity of the wound, initial injury signals may vary, triggering a differential requirement for stem cell division and regulatory signaling pathways.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing pharynx and eye regeneration requirements.

claim: F-ara-EdU-labeled stem cells are differentially incorporated into regenerating and non-regenerating tissues depending on when they are labeled relative to injury.
source: Also, the timing of experimentation and analysis should be deliberate, as we show that F-ara-EdU-labeled stem cells are differentially incorporated into regenerating and non-regenerating tissues depending on when they are labeled relative to injury.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from F-ara-EdU labeling experiments at different time points.

claim: Stem cells identified by piwi-1 and H3P staining encompass cells with different potencies and differentiation states.
source: Stem cells identified by piwi-1 and H3P staining encompass cells with different potencies and differentiation states (van Wolfswinkel et al., 2014; Zeng et al., 2018), which may respond uniquely to the changing environment of a regenerating animal.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Broad analysis of stem cells lacks the resolution required to tease apart the intricacies involved in coordinating regeneration.
source: Therefore, broad analysis of stem cells lacks the resolution required to tease apart the intricacies involved in coordinating regeneration.
evidence: This is an inference based on the heterogeneity of stem cell populations.

claim: Heterogeneity exists even within subsets of organ-specific progenitors.
source: However, our observation of the asymmetric and symmetric segregation of FoxA in dividing cells suggests that heterogeneity exists even within these subsets of stem cells.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from observations of FoxA distribution during cell division.

claim: Phosphorylation of ERK promotes regeneration in many animals.
source: Phosphorylation of ERK promotes regeneration in many animals (DuBuc et al., 2014; Wan et al., 2012; Yun et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: In planaria, ERK has been implicated as a regeneration trigger, as it is briefly activated by phosphorylation within minutes of injury.
source: In planaria, ERK has been implicated as a regeneration trigger, as it is briefly activated by phosphorylation within minutes of injury and is required for wound-induced transcription, stem cell differentiation and broad stem cell proliferation (Owlarn et al., 2017; Tasaki et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: ERK functions to re-establish axial patterning during regeneration.
source: ERK also functions to re-establish axial patterning during regeneration (Owlarn et al., 2017; Umesono et al., 2013), which depends on a network of positional cues that are expressed in muscle cells throughout the body (Lander and Petersen, 2016; Scimone et al., 2016; Witchley et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Tissue removal from the body requires re-establishment of positional cues for regeneration to proceed.
source: Because tissue removal from the body requires re-establishment of these positional cues for regeneration to proceed (Rink, 2018), it has been difficult to distinguish ERK's roles in organ regeneration.
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Pharynx removal does not broadly disrupt positional cues.
source: Unlike amputations to the body, pharynx removal does not broadly disrupt positional cues, which has allowed us to pinpoint a distinct role for ERK in organ regeneration.
evidence: This is an inference based on the anatomical isolation of the pharynx.

claim: Both ERK activity and stem cell division act simultaneously, but independently, 1–2 days after pharynx loss, to drive the expansion of pharynx progenitors 3 days after amputation.
source: Both ERK activity and stem cell division act simultaneously, but independently, 1–2 days after pharynx loss, to drive the expansion of pharynx progenitors 3 days after amputation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from drug treatment experiments showing independent effects.

claim: An ERK-independent signal triggers division of FoxA+ stem cells.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that an ERK-independent signal triggers division of FoxA+ stem cells, and that ERK acts later during organ regeneration to facilitate stem cell differentiation or maintain cell fate.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation that ERK does not affect progenitor division.

claim: ERK acts later during organ regeneration to facilitate stem cell differentiation or maintain cell fate.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that an ERK-independent signal triggers division of FoxA+ stem cells, and that ERK acts later during organ regeneration to facilitate stem cell differentiation or maintain cell fate.
evidence: This is speculation based on the timing and effects of ERK inhibition.

claim: Both ERK and fst are absolutely essential for regeneration following substantial anterior tissue removal, but become less so if smaller amounts of tissue are removed.
source: Interestingly, both ERK and fst are absolutely essential for regeneration following substantial anterior tissue removal, but become less so if smaller amounts of tissue are removed.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and previous studies.

claim: The variability in ERK and fst requirements may be due to the extent of axial patterning disruption induced by different amputations.
source: This variability may be due to the extent of axial patterning disruption induced by different amputations.
evidence: This is speculation based on the relationship between tissue removal and patterning.

claim: The inability of fst(RNAi) animals to regenerate is entirely dependent on their failure to reset positional information.
source: In fact, the inability of fst(RNAi) animals to regenerate is entirely dependent on their failure to reset positional information, as inhibition of wnt signals that restrict head formation rescue these regeneration defects (Tewari et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tewari et al., 2018.

claim: Injury-induced fst expression and ERK phosphorylation primarily regulate regeneration initiation by establishing repatterning rather than triggering stem cell behaviors that directly contribute to organ regeneration.
source: Therefore, it is likely that injury-induced fst expression and ERK phosphorylation primarily regulate regeneration initiation by establishing repatterning rather than triggering stem cell behaviors that directly contribute to organ regeneration.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the relationship between fst, ERK, and patterning.

claim: Not all injury-induced stem cell behaviors may be critical for regeneration.
source: ERK inhibition reduces broad stem cell division after tissue removal (Owlarn et al., 2017), but not the specific increase in division of pharynx progenitors that accompanies pharynx loss, suggesting that not all injury-induced stem cell behaviors may be critical for regeneration.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the differential effects of ERK inhibition.

claim: Rescuing axial repatterning after fst knockdown does not rescue defects in missing tissue-induced stem cell proliferation and apoptosis.
source: Further, rescuing axial repatterning, and thus regeneration after fst knockdown, does not rescue defects in missing tissue-induced stem cell proliferation and apoptosis (Tewari et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tewari et al., 2018.

claim: The 'missing-tissue response' may encompass multiple events including patterning, broad stem cell division, and the generation of organ-specific progenitors that contribute independently to different aspects of regeneration.
source: Therefore, the 'missing-tissue response' may encompass multiple events including patterning, broad stem cell division, and the generation of organ-specific progenitors that contribute independently to different aspects of regeneration.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the independent effects of different regeneration mechanisms.

claim: Receptor tyrosine kinases such as EGFR and FGFR have been shown to play critical roles in signaling upstream of ERK in many organisms.
source: Receptor tyrosine kinases such as the epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) and the fibroblast growth factor receptor (FGFR) have been shown to play critical roles in signaling upstream of ERK in many organisms (Patel and Shvartsman, 2018), making them intriguing candidates for potential regulators of regeneration.
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: In planarians, egfr-3 is required to activate ERK during regeneration.
source: In planarians, egfr-3 is required to activate ERK during regeneration (Fraguas et al., 2017) and is also involved in stem cell differentiation (Fraguas et al., 2011; Lei et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The ligand egf-4 and the receptors egfr-1 and egfr-5 are involved in the differentiation of stem cells into brain, intestinal and excretory tissues, respectively.
source: Other studies have highlighted roles for the ligand egf-4 and the receptors egfr-1 and egfr-5 in the differentiation of stem cells into brain, intestinal and excretory tissues, respectively (Barberán et al., 2016; Fraguas et al., 2014; Rink et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Some FGFRL-Wnt circuits restrict pharynx formation to the trunk region, possibly through regulation of FoxA expression.
source: Further, some FGFRL-Wnt circuits restrict pharynx formation to the trunk region, possibly through regulation of FoxA expression (Lander and Petersen, 2016; Scimone et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Both the overall number of FoxA+ pharynx progenitors, as well as those that are actively dividing, increase only after pharynx removal.
source: Intriguingly, we find that both the overall number of FoxA+ pharynx progenitors, as well as those that are actively dividing, increase only after pharynx removal.
evidence: This is a summary of experimental findings on pharynx progenitor dynamics.

claim: Stem cells sense the absence of the pharynx and channel their proliferative output toward the population of stem cells required to regenerate it.
source: Therefore, stem cells sense the absence of the pharynx and channel their proliferative output toward the population of stem cells required to regenerate it.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experimental data on selective pharynx progenitor responses.

claim: The heterogeneity of the stem cell population can be differentially deployed depending on the severity of the injury and the particular tissues that need repair.
source: Combined with our analysis of non-pharyngeal progenitor dynamics after different amputations, our results suggest that the heterogeneity of the stem cell population can be differentially deployed depending on the severity of the injury and the particular tissues that need repair.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experimental data on multiple progenitor types.

claim: Removal of non-pharyngeal tissues like the head does not increase pharynx progenitor proliferation but nevertheless results in increased F-ara EdU+ cells within the pharynx.
source: Interestingly, removal of non-pharyngeal tissues like the head, does not increase pharynx progenitor proliferation but nevertheless results in increased F-ara EdU+ cells within the pharynx, raising a conundrum regarding the source of these cells.
evidence: This is an observation from experimental data that raises a question.

claim: Non-FoxA+ progenitors which have yet to be identified may contribute to pharynx regeneration.
source: One possibility is that other, non-FoxA+ progenitors which have yet to be identified, may contribute to pharynx regeneration.
evidence: This is speculation about potential alternative progenitor sources.

claim: No other tissue-specific transcription factors or proposed pharynx progenitor markers appear to be required for pharynx regeneration.
source: However, no other tissue-specific transcription factors or proposed pharynx progenitor markers (meis, twist, or dd_554) appear to be required for pharynx regeneration (Cowles et al., 2013; Scimone et al., 2014a; Zhu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Planarian stem cells, even those expressing organ-specific transcription factors, may harbor a large degree of plasticity that allows fate switching between stem cell and progenitor types.
source: Alternatively, a recent study has suggested that planarian stem cells, even those expressing organ-specific transcription factors, may harbor a large degree of plasticity that allows fate switching between stem cell and progenitor types (Raz et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Raz et al., 2021.

claim: Stem cells generated soon after tissue loss could adopt a pharynx progenitor fate at various times over the course of regeneration, which would not necessarily generate a detectable increase in pharynx progenitors at any one time.
source: While this hypothesis has not been tested in the context of injury, it is possible that stem cells generated soon after tissue loss could adopt a pharynx progenitor fate at various times over the course of regeneration, which would not necessarily generate a detectable increase in pharynx progenitors at any one time.
evidence: This is speculation about potential mechanisms of progenitor generation.

claim: Stem cell division in a narrow window, 1–2 days following pharynx amputation, is absolutely essential for pharynx regeneration.
source: Surprisingly, stem cell division in a narrow window, 1–2 days following pharynx amputation, is absolutely essential for pharynx regeneration, and coincides with the elevation of pharynx progenitor division that directly precedes their increase 3 days after pharynx amputation.
evidence: This is a major finding supported by nocodazole treatment experiments.

claim: The requirement for division in a brief moment after amputation suggests that stem cells detect tissue loss through transient signals regulated by injury.
source: The requirement for division in this brief moment after amputation suggests that stem cells detect tissue loss through transient signals regulated by injury.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the temporal specificity of division requirements.

claim: A population of potentially slow-cycling stem cells, reminiscent of reserve stem cells in mammals, may be specifically induced to enter the cell cycle by tissue loss.
source: Indeed, a recent study has identified a population of potentially slow-cycling stem cells, reminiscent of reserve stem cells in mammals, that may be specifically induced to enter the cell cycle by tissue loss (Bankaitis et al., 2018; Molinaro et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Regulatory signals could either be produced upon injury to promote regeneration, or released from inhibitory cues that might emanate from organs when they are present.
source: Regulatory signals could either be produced upon injury to promote regeneration, or released from inhibitory cues that might emanate from organs when they are present (Rink, 2018; Ziller-Sengel, 1967; Ziller-Sengel, 1965).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The majority of transient amputation-induced transcriptional changes occur within differentiated cell types.
source: Intriguingly, a recent study characterizing transient amputation-induced transcriptional changes revealed that the majority of these changes occur within differentiated cell types (Benham-Pyle et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Benham-Pyle et al., 2020.

claim: The possibility of transient signals customized to particular organs and the ability of stem cells to readily sense them may explain how planarians exhibit such rapid and robust regeneration of all organs.
source: The possibility of transient signals customized to particular organs and the ability of stem cells to readily sense them may explain how planarians exhibit such rapid and robust regeneration of all organs.
evidence: This is speculation based on the findings of the study.

claim: Cell fate acquisition can occur throughout the cell cycle.
source: Cell fate acquisition can occur throughout the cell cycle (Fichelson et al., 2005; Pauklin and Vallier, 2014; Soufi and Dalton, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The increase in FoxA expression in both actively dividing stem cells, and those outside of M-phase, does not pinpoint a particular time in the cell cycle where fate acquisition during regeneration might occur.
source: The increase in FoxA expression in both actively dividing stem cells, and those outside of M-phase, does not pinpoint a particular time in the cell cycle where fate acquisition during regeneration might occur.
evidence: This is an observation from experimental data.

claim: Tissue loss could generate fleeting signals sensed by stem cells that influence them to adopt a specific cell fate during division to compensate for missing tissue.
source: Tissue loss could generate fleeting signals sensed by stem cells that influence them to adopt a specific cell fate during division to compensate for missing tissue.
evidence: This is speculation about potential mechanisms of fate acquisition.

claim: Stem cells already expressing organ-specific markers may be poised to divide upon receiving a signal, allowing them to quickly initiate regeneration upon exit of the cell cycle.
source: Alternatively, stem cells already expressing organ-specific markers may be poised to divide upon receiving such a signal, allowing them to quickly initiate regeneration upon exit of the cell cycle.
evidence: This is speculation about potential mechanisms of progenitor activation.

claim: FoxA1 remains attached to chromatin during mitosis, contributing to rapid activation of downstream targets following mitosis during liver differentiation.
source: Indeed, studies in human hepatoma cell lines have shown that FoxA1 remains attached to chromatin during mitosis, contributing to rapid activation of downstream targets following mitosis during liver differentiation (Caravaca et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Caravaca et al., 2013.

claim: Mammalian homologs of FoxA were the first identified 'pioneer' transcription factors, characterized by their ability to engage closed chromatin and drive organogenesis.
source: Mammalian homologs of FoxA were the first identified 'pioneer' transcription factors, characterized by their ability to engage closed chromatin and drive organogenesis (Hsu et al., 2015; Iwafuchi-Doi and Zaret, 2016; Lam et al., 2013; Zaret and Mango, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Pioneer factors may be viable in vivo targets for achieving regeneration of entire organs.
source: This raises the possibility that pioneer factors may be viable in vivo targets for achieving regeneration of entire organs.
evidence: This is speculation based on the properties of pioneer factors.

claim: Overexpression of FoxN is sufficient to drive regeneration of the thymus in mice.
source: In fact, overexpression of a related mammalian transcription factor, FoxN, is sufficient to drive regeneration of the thymus in mice (Bredenkamp et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bredenkamp et al., 2014.

claim: The increased proliferation of stem cells expressing FoxA after pharynx removal suggests that activation of pioneer factors may also drive organ regeneration in planaria.
source: The increased proliferation of stem cells expressing FoxA after pharynx removal suggests that activation of pioneer factors may also drive organ regeneration in planaria.
evidence: This is speculation based on experimental findings and knowledge of pioneer factors.

claim: Other pioneer factors, including gata-4/5/6, soxB1-2 and FoxD, are also expressed in planarian stem cells and are required for regeneration of the intestine, sensory neurons, and anterior pole, respectively.
source: Other pioneer factors, including gata-4/5/6, soxB1-2 and FoxD, are also expressed in planarian stem cells and are required for regeneration of the intestine (Flores et al., 2016; González-Sastre et al., 2017), sensory neurons (Ross et al., 2018), and anterior pole (Scimone et al., 2014b; Vogg et al., 2014), respectively.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Upregulation of pioneer factors in stem cells may be a general strategy used to initiate organ regeneration.
source: Therefore, upregulation of pioneer factors in stem cells may be a general strategy used to initiate organ regeneration.
evidence: This is speculation based on the role of multiple pioneer factors in regeneration.

claim: Identifying the regulatory mechanisms responsible for the selective activation of pioneer factors in stem cells may be an ideal approach to understanding how organisms initiate regeneration of targeted organs in vivo.
source: Identifying the regulatory mechanisms responsible for the selective activation of pioneer factors in stem cells may be an ideal approach to understanding how organisms initiate regeneration of targeted organs in vivo.
evidence: This is a proposal for future research based on the findings of the study.
